chapter: Hampton band, Honolulu and the war years
title: Bernard Banks's band in Honolulu
summary: He takes a $35-a-week dance hall job in Honolulu with Bernard Banks, brings his wife, and names band members including Henry Coker.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: In September I received a job to go to Honolulu--this is
at the same time that I was working on that $17.50 job.
That was a new offer?
New offer.
This offer was from Bernard Banks, the pianist who was taking a group to Honolulu to play in a dancehall there.
Wasn't Bernard Banks the brother of Buddy Banks?
That's right.
Who played saxophone and later piano?
That's right.
I was attracted because the money was good and the job was steady.
How was that good? What do you mean?
$35.00 a week
That was a far cry from the $17.50; wasn't it? And Hawaii too.
I took my wife with me and I left our daughter with her

grandmother in Los Angeles. After three months, my wife's mother passed and she came back to Los Angeles for the funeral and then she had to bring our daughter back with her. She was only eleven years old at that time; this is 1936, in January.

Our band went over very big in dance halls Honolulu at the / and so our boss took advantage of it and booked us on private jobs. We didn't care about that because we were still getting our $35.00 a week.
You made some extra too then; didn't you?
He gave us a little extra.
Our personnel was Henry Coker (unintelligible spelling), Kirk Bradford, Leon Scott, Bill Winston; those were musicians who were famous back in Chicago in the thirties.
The name Henry Coker,
the late Henry Coker, later had a stint with the Count Basie Band; didn't he?
That's right, he worked ten years with Count Basie.
And also married Marie Dickerson that we mentioned earlier.
That's right, Marie Dickerson, she was a pilot.
Yes, an aviatrix.
